episode_title: The Ruler Who Executed His Own Family to Save His Son's Throne: Hideyoshi's Final, Darkest Years
youtube_title: He Wiped Out His Own Family to Save a Toddler's Throne. It Lasted 20 Years.
youtube_description:
In 1595, the ruler of Japan ordered his own nephew's wives and children killed on a Kyoto riverbank. Toyotomi Hideyoshi had conquered an entire country, yet one small child's future frightened him enough to destroy his own family. Was Hidetsugu a real threat, or a victim of an old man's fear? We follow Hideyoshi's darkest decision, and what it cost the house he was trying to save.

Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent whose grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to a single day in Japan's past. He can watch and speak, but he can never change what happens.

teaser_narration: A Kyoto riverbank, a grey sky, and a silent crowd. I stand among them. The ruler of Japan has ordered his own nephew's family killed. Why would the man who conquered everything destroy the family he chose? I'm Tokio Kamiya, and the answer begins with one small child.

scenes.narration: I'm Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent. My grandfather, a Kyoto clockmaker, left me a brass pocket watch, and it carries me to any moment in Japan's past, one day at a time. I can watch and speak, but I can never change a thing. For this report, the watch sets me down first above Odawara, in 1590. Armies fill the plain, and on a platform stands a small, wiry man in golden armor: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, son of a poor farmer or foot soldier; the sources do not agree. His victory over the Hojo will bring all of Japan under one hand, and he already holds the title of kampaku, the emperor's chief adviser. Yet for most of his life he has had no son, and the boy he finally has is still a baby. That fragile hope will shape everything that follows.

scenes.narration: My watch gives me no day in 1589, so I turn to the records. That year, when Hideyoshi is in his early fifties, his consort Yodo-dono gives birth to a boy named Tsurumatsu. Hideyoshi's letters from this period show a doting, delighted father. I picture him in a gilded chamber, cradling the infant. He begins to imagine a lasting house, a Toyotomi line that will rule for generations. The man who rose from nothing finally has something worth protecting. Then, in 1591, the child falls gravely ill.

scenes.narration: I read the next part in the records, too. Early in 1591, Hideyoshi's younger brother Hidenaga, the calm partner who steadied his rise for decades, dies. Months later, in the eighth month, little Tsurumatsu dies as well, not yet three years old. Accounts say Hideyoshi is inconsolable and cuts off his topknot in grief. At fifty-four, with no son and one fewer trusted ally, he begins to see that his empire might not outlive him. And I think a ruler who sees that is a dangerous thing.

scenes.narration: On another day, in the twelfth month of 1591, I watch from the back of a grand hall. Hideyoshi has turned to his family. He has adopted his nephew Toyotomi Hidetsugu, son of his sister Tomo, a man in his early twenties, and now hands him the title of kampaku. Hideyoshi becomes taiko, the retired regent, but keeps real power in his own hands. Hidetsugu receives the grand Jurakudai palace in Kyoto and an unspoken promise: one day, all of Japan will be his.

scenes.narration: On a quiet afternoon, I am allowed a glimpse of the new kampaku at Jurakudai. Hidetsugu unrolls an old manuscript while scholars kneel nearby. He receives nobles, presides over the court, collects old texts and entertains poets. But later chronicles paint another portrait. They call him the Sessho Kampaku, the Killing Regent, and accuse him of cruelty, even of cutting down innocent people for sport. Most of those stories come from accounts written after his death, often by authors with reason to justify his fall. How much of it is true, historians still argue.

scenes.narration: For 1593, I follow the records. With the Korean campaign dragging on, word reaches Hideyoshi at his war headquarters in Kyushu: Yodo-dono has given birth to another son, named Hideyori. Hideyoshi, now fifty-six, leaves the war behind and hurries home to Osaka. I picture him striding down a gilded corridor, his tired face bright with hope. His letters again show a giddy, devoted father. And Hidetsugu, the heir who was such a convenient answer, becomes a different kind of problem.

scenes.narration: On another day, I kneel among the retainers at the dark edge of a lamplit hall. Hideyoshi and Hidetsugu sit across from each other, an empty cushion between them. According to some accounts, Hideyoshi wants a peaceful arrangement: a marriage between Hideyori and Hidetsugu's daughter, and talk of dividing authority between them. But I find it hard to see how that could last. Hidetsugu is a grown man, already kampaku, with his own retainers and allies. Hideyori is an infant. Every nobleman in Japan can count the years until the boy grows up.

scenes.narration: Fushimi Castle, summer, 1595. The arrangement has collapsed, and Hidetsugu stands accused of plotting rebellion. From the end of a corridor, I watch him wait outside closed doors. A foot soldier on duty told me the stories going around: oaths the kampaku supposedly swore, allies he supposedly gathered. He also told me Hidetsugu has sent a written oath of loyalty and come when summoned. Yet he is refused an audience. Whether he truly planned revolt, or the charge is a pretext, the sources do not settle.

scenes.narration: I do not go to that temple. The records say that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, at Seigan-ji temple, Toyotomi Hidetsugu takes his own life. Most accounts say Hideyoshi ordered it; some historians now argue he chose death to protest his innocence. He is in his late twenties. Several of his young retainers die with him. His head is sent to Kyoto. The man who named him kampaku four years ago has now destroyed him. But Hideyoshi is not finished. In the logic of the age, a surviving family can become a banner for revolt.

scenes.narration: On the second day of the eighth month, I stand far back among townspeople on the Kamo riverbank at Sanjo in Kyoto. I can watch, and nothing more. Hidetsugu's wives, concubines and children are brought out to die. There are dozens of them. From where I stand, I cannot see the platform clearly; accounts say his head is displayed before them. Most are women, many very young. Some have barely arrived in the capital. Others hardly knew him. The crowd around me is silent. And the order comes from the ruler of Japan.

scenes.narration: Later that year, the watch sets me down in Kyoto again. Workmen on ladders are pulling gold-leaf panels from Jurakudai. The destruction has not stopped with people. Hideyoshi has ordered his own magnificent palace, the home of Hidetsugu's court, torn down. Much of the material is reused elsewhere, including at Fushimi. I watch one of the most luxurious buildings in Japan disappear. Hidetsugu's lands are seized, and what was his household is scattered.

scenes.narration: From the far end of a great hall, I watch the lords of Japan kneel in two long lines. Hideyoshi demands that they swear, in writing, to serve Hideyori after him. Tokugawa Ieyasu, Maeda Toshiie, Mori Terumoto and many others sign oaths, and over the following years some are made to renew them. They promise to obey Hideyori's authority and Hideyoshi's laws. The signatures are meant to be unbreakable. The man who has just destroyed his own family's branch now trusts paper to protect his child.

scenes.narration: Spring, 1598, and I walk among hundreds of guests in silk under the cherry trees at Daigo temple. It looks like triumph. To me, it looks like a farewell. This summer, he will create a council of Five Elders and Five Commissioners to govern in the boy's name, and his health will soon fail.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Think about what Hideyoshi actually chose. He could have kept Hidetsugu as protector for the infant, bound by blood and oath. Instead he removed the one grown man of his own family who might have guarded the boy, and put his trust in the oaths of rivals. Every lord who signed knew what happened to a relative who stood in the way. They also knew the old man was dying. scenes.narration: Reporter's note. So was Hidetsugu a danger or a victim? I don't think the sources let us say for certain. Accounts from Hideyoshi's own circle lean toward danger. Many modern researchers doubt that the rebellion charge was strong, and suspect the cruelty stories were exaggerated afterward. What no one disputes is the outcome. Near the Sanjo bridge in Kyoto, a small temple still keeps graves for Hidetsugu's family. One man's fear of an uncertain future produced a certain tragedy, and the family it was meant to protect did not last the generation.

scenes.narration: Hideyoshi began as a peasant's son and ended as a father terrified of his own mortality. He won nearly every war he fought for power, and lost the only one that mattered. I think the choice he made at Sanjo shows how often rulers destroy what they love in the name of protecting it. There are more stories like his in Japanese history, and I would like to meet them with you. If you want to come along, you know where to find us. The watch is ticking. Until the next report. Tokio Kamiya, reporting.
